response.title: Which affordable 3D scanner works well with a home 3D printer for copying broken plastic parts and printing replacements?
response.answer:
For copying broken plastic parts and printing replacements with a home 3D printer, I'd focus on 3D scanners in the $200–$600 range.

My top choices are Creality CR-Scan Ferret Pro, 3DMakerpro Moose Lite, and Revopoint INSPIRE.

But there's an important distinction: a scanner that produces a beautiful 3D model isn't necessarily good at reproducing a mechanical part accurately.

For replacement parts such as appliance clips, plastic brackets, hinges, covers, and mounting tabs, you need accurate dimensions, screw-hole locations, and flat surfaces—not just a detailed scan.

A good workflow is:

Scan

Measure & CAD

3D print

Best scanners to consider
My pick for small parts

3DMakerpro Seal Lite

$359.00

Claimed 0.02 mm accuracy. Blue structured light is suited to capturing small, detailed components such as clips, knobs, and plastic fittings. Less versatile for large objects.

Seller: B&H Photo

Best all-around budget choice

3DMakerpro - Moose Lite Handheld 3D Scanner for 3D Printing,…

$369.99

Claimed 0.05 mm accuracy. Good for scanning a variety of household parts, brackets, and housings. Markerless tracking and broader size coverage.

Seller: Best Buy

Creality CR-Scan Ferret Pro

$299.00

Claimed 0.1 mm accuracy. Wireless and portable, good for medium-sized covers and larger household objects. Not my first choice for tiny snap-fit features.

Seller: Creality Official Store · Promotional listing

Revopoint INSPIRE 2

$566.00

Claimed 0.05 mm accuracy. Hybrid infrared laser and structured-light scanning make it a versatile option for household repair work, including challenging surfaces.

Seller: Revopoint 3D US

Prices are current listings and may change. Accuracy numbers are manufacturer claims, not guaranteed accuracy on every printed replacement. 
3D Printing
+1
What actually works when copying broken parts?

A common misconception is that you can scan a broken part, export an STL, and immediately print an identical replacement.

Sometimes you can, but for functional components you'll usually need to repair or remodel the geometry.

For example:

Broken clip: Scan the remaining shape, then reconstruct the missing tab in CAD.

Plastic gear: Measure the teeth, bore, and dimensions. CAD reconstruction is generally more reliable than directly printing a scan.

Appliance cover: Scanning is particularly useful because the curved surfaces can be difficult to model manually.

Mounting bracket: Calipers and CAD may be faster and more accurate than scanning.

For software, consider FreeCAD or Fusion for rebuilding the part, and Blender or MeshLab for cleaning the scan. A standard STL or OBJ mesh is not automatically an editable parametric CAD model.

My recommendation

If your main purpose is repairing household items, I'd choose the 3DMakerpro Seal Lite for small plastic parts or the Moose Lite if your parts vary considerably in size.

Before spending money, one question would help me narrow this down considerably:

What size are the parts you typically want to copy?
Tiny clips, gears, or fittings (under 2 inches)
Typical household parts (2–8 inches)
Larger appliance panels or housings (over 8 inches)
What's your scanner budget?
Under $200
$200–$300
$300–$500

search_results.snippet: This guide reviews the best 3D scanners for creating accurate digital models of real-world objects, covering options for beginners, professionals and specialist applications. The overall winner is the Revopoint Miraco Plus, offering 0.04mm accuracy, versatile scanning capabilities and photogrammetric metrology features, although its $1,799–$2,119 price makes it best suited to serious hobbyists and professionals. Other recommendations include the affordable Revopoint Inspire ($449) for beginners, the 3DMakerPro Eagle for value-focused LiDAR scanning of large spaces, and the Creality Sermoon P1
